sheet-9.description: Sheet 9 covers the residential and institutional blocks of Bridgeton north of East Commerce Street and east of North Pearl Street, drawn at 50 feet to an inch with a compass rose at the right. North Pearl Street runs down the left side, Bank Street down the middle and Walnut Street along the right, with Washington Street crossing the sheet about halfway down, Cedar Street on the right half, and East Commerce Street running diagonally across the bottom. Church Lane and Elmer Street enter from the left and top edges. The blocks are mostly detached frame dwellings with outbuildings, laid out in long narrow lots, with a few frame houses in the upper right. Public buildings stand in the middle and lower part of the sheet: the Bank Street Public School and its annex, a public school annex for manual training and domestic science, a Masonic Hall, Christ's English Lutheran Church, the Second Presbyterian Church, the Central M. E. Church and its chapel, and the Post Office, a fireproof building put up in 1910 at the corner of East Commerce Street and Walnut Street. A small lane named Walnut Place runs off Walnut Street at the right. A row of small stores and shops fronts East Commerce Street at the lower left. The area left of North Pearl Street and the large blocks at the right, beyond Walnut Street, are left blank, being drawn on sheets 8, 2, 3 and 10, and the margins also name sheets 7, 12, 8A and 8B. Water mains of four, six, eight, ten and sixteen inches are marked in the streets, and fire hydrants and fire alarm boxes stand at the corners.
notes: Printed N. Pearl, E. Commerce and Bank are North Pearl Street, East Commerce Street (Commerce Street East near Bank Street and Orange Street in OpenStreetMap) and Bank Street.
Walnut Place is not in the OpenStreetMap extract.
The sheet scan is about 2 percent larger than sheets 2 to 8, so its fitted px_per_ft is 8.02 against about 7.86 on the others.

Detected control: eight junctions on Washington, Bank, Cedar, Walnut, Orange and Commerce streets; the junctions of Elmer Street with Walnut Street and Pine Street with East Commerce Street were not detected.
map, 50 ft: Washington, Bank, Cedar, Walnut, E. Commerce; scan about 2 percent wider than the others

sheet-10.description: Sheet 10 covers a residential district of Bridgeton east of the Cohansey River, the three blocks numbered 121, 122 and 123 between Walnut Street on the west and Church Street on the east, running from Marion Street at the top of the sheet south to East Commerce Street at the bottom. Elmer Street and Cedar Street cross the sheet from west to east, so each block is a long strip of lots facing the two streets that bound it. A diagonal Private Way runs south-east through the lower block from Cedar Street towards East Commerce Street, and the short Walnut Place leads east off Walnut Street near the bottom of the sheet. Pine Street appears at the lower left corner, meeting East Commerce Street. The drawing is almost entirely detached frame dwellings, most of two or two and a half storeys, each with a small auto house or outbuilding at the rear of its lot; there is one brick building near East Commerce Street and a few concrete block garages, but no factories, churches or schools. Six inch water pipes run in Walnut Street, Elmer Street and Cedar Street, a sixteen inch main in East Commerce Street, and fire hydrants and a fire alarm box stand at the corners. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch. The south side of East Commerce Street and the area east of Church Street are left blank, being drawn on the adjoining sheets 7 and 11; sheets 12, 13 and 9 adjoin to the north-west, north and west.
notes: Detector settings piloted on this sheet: ink_below_paper 45.
map, 50 ft: pilot; Walnut to Church, Marion to E. Commerce

sheet-11.description: Sheet 11 shows a residential district in the east of Bridgeton between Church on the west, East Commerce at the bottom and the shore of East Lake along the right edge. Marion, Elmer and Cedar run across the sheet from Church and meet North East Avenue, which crosses the map diagonally from the top centre to the bottom and divides the blocks numbered 124, 125 and 126 on its west side from blocks 114, 120 and 38 on its east side. Linden and Yorke are the main cross streets east of North East Avenue. Almost all of the buildings are detached frame dwellings of two or two and a half storeys, each with small outbuildings, set in regular lots; there are a few brick-coloured dwellings and a handful of buildings in blue for concrete block construction. At the lower left a bake shop with two ovens stands on block 126 beside a row of long narrow sheds, and near East Commerce a larger building marked as a dwelling with brick walls stands at the centre. East Lake is a pale blue pond with an irregular shoreline curving down the right edge of the sheet, continuing as a stream with two bridges that loops round a large tile-roofed building at the bottom right; Lake Breeze Cottage is labelled beside it, and a retaining wall is marked along the lower edge. Six inch water pipes run in the streets and sixteen inch and twelve inch pipes in East Commerce. A compass with a north arrow is drawn near the lake. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch. Adjoining sheets 10, 13, 7 and 38 are named in the margins.
notes: Modern OpenStreetMap names: North East Avenue is East Avenue and Yorke is York Street; Marion, Elmer, Cedar, Church, Linden and East Commerce are Marion Street, Elmer Street, Cedar Street, Church Street, Linden Street and East Commerce Street.
The labelled building near the lake at the bottom right is marked Tile on the sheet.
map, 50 ft: Church, Marion, Elmer, Cedar, E. Commerce, N. East Av, Linden, Yorke

sheet-12.description: Sheet 12 covers a district of north-central Bridgeton on the east side of the town between North Pearl at the left edge and Church at the upper right. Irving Avenue crosses the upper part of the sheet diagonally from lower left to upper right, and Bank, Walnut and Marion run through the middle, with Parker crossing Walnut in the east and Elmer Street appearing at the bottom right. The north arrow and compass are drawn at the upper left and the sheet is turned about 25 degrees from north. The most prominent building complex is the E. Pritchard Tomato Canning and Ketchup Factory on the south side of Irving Avenue, a cluster of cooking, labelling and packing rooms, storage and warehouse buildings drawn in pink and yellow with their floor uses lettered, standing between Bank and a cemetery. The Pearl St. Baptist Church, a pink brick building with its heating and lighting noted, stands on the cemetery tract at the left, which is block 106 and is otherwise open. Between Bank and Walnut, and again east of Walnut and north and south of Parker, the blocks numbered 107, 116 and 117 are lined with detached frame dwellings of two or two and a half storeys with small outbuildings. At the bottom left a sausage factory stands among dwellings south of Marion. Six, eight and twelve inch water pipes run in the streets, and fire alarm boxes and telephone hydrants mark many corners. The blocks beyond Walnut at the lower right are blank and belong to sheet 10. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch. Neighbouring sheets named in the margins are 16 and 17 at the top, 13 at the right, 10 and 9 at the bottom, and 14, 8 and 7 to the west.
notes: The modern OpenStreetMap node of Marion Street and North Pearl Street lies about 10 m from the parcel right-of-way centre and gave a poor fit; it was left out of the control.

Modern names: North Pearl is North Pearl Street (also tagged Pearl Street North in OpenStreetMap), Bank, Walnut, Church, Marion and Parker are Bank Street, Walnut Street, Church Street, Marion Street and Parker Street.
The Parker Street / Walnut Street and Elmer Street / Walnut Street control points were hand-picked at the water pipe corners.
map, 50 ft: Walnut, Parker, Elmer, N. Pearl; Marion / N. Pearl left out (modern Marion bends at Bank, 23 m off)

sheet-13.description: Sheet 13 shows a residential district of Bridgeton north-east of the town centre, bounded by Irving Avenue along the top, Church on the left and Yorke on the right, with North East Avenue running down the middle of the sheet and Marion and Wood crossing near the bottom. The sheet is turned slightly from north, as the compass at the right shows. Four long blocks of detached frame dwellings, mostly two or two and a half storeys, each with a small outbuilding at the rear of its lot, fill the area between these streets: block 115 between Church and North East Avenue, block 119 between North East Avenue and Yorke, and block 120 east of Yorke with its lots running back towards the margin. Several dwellings are tinted pink for brick, and a few outbuildings blue for concrete block. The one open area is a large playground in block 114 south of Wood, drawn almost empty apart from an outhouse, with a few dwellings along its south and east sides. Parker is drawn at the left edge beside the lower-left corner, where a small group of dwellings numbered from the 90s to the 120s on the side of Church is shown from block 116. At the top right the area marked 35 is blank and drawn on that sheet, and a dash-dot match line is drawn near the right edge with lettered corners. Six inch water pipes run in the streets, with a four inch pipe in Parker, and fire alarm boxes and telephone hydrants stand at corners. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch. Adjoining sheets named in the margins are 17 at the top, 12 at the lower left, 10, 11 at the bottom and 35 at the right.
notes: Modern names: North East Avenue is East Avenue and Yorke is York Street in OpenStreetMap; Church, Parker, Wood and Marion are Church Street, Parker Street, Wood Street and Marion Street.
A dash-dot line near the right edge, lettered A and B at its ends, is a match line with sheet 35.
map, 50 ft: East Av, Wood and neighbours

sheet-14.description: Sheet 14 covers the part of Bridgeton on the east bank of the Cohansey River, from the river and the Central Railroad of New Jersey yards at the left across to North Pearl at the right edge. Cohansey runs down the page beside the tracks and is crossed at right angles by Laning near the top and by Irving Avenue at the middle, while North Laurel and North Pearl run down the page in the east, with Rose, Myrtle Street and Marion crossing them. Irving Avenue bends north-east on the east side of North Laurel and runs diagonally across the blocks numbered 105 and 110. The compass at the left shows the sheet turned about 25 degrees from north. Beside the tracks stand the Municipal Garage, with its wagon shed and storage of apparatus, a Section House, and a long C.R.R. of N.J. Produce House drawn along the sidings, with the notes Top of High Bank and No Exposure lettered along the river side. Between Cohansey and North Laurel are blocks 101 and 3, with rows of dwellings, a coal and wood yard, a sheet metal shop and a hay and feed store, a sausage factory, a warehouse marked cement floor and a hay shed. East of North Laurel are detached frame dwellings, a brick church marked 1st, a wholesale grocery on Irving Avenue and a short Myrtle Terrace at the top right. Water pipes of six and eight inches run in the streets. The Cohansey River is tinted blue at the lower left, with a concrete coal trestle crossing the tracks. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch. Adjoining sheets named in the margins are 15 and 16 above, 16 and 12 at the right, and 2, 3, 6 and 8 below.
notes: Modern OpenStreetMap names: Laning is Lanning Street, North Laurel is North Laurel Street, North Pearl is North Pearl Street (also tagged Pearl Street North), Cohansey is Cohansey Street, Rose is Rose Street and Marion is Marion Street.
Marion Street is lettered both Marion across the lower part and Marion St. at the right edge; Myrtle Terrace is not in OpenStreetMap.
map, 50 ft: N. Pearl, Laning (Lanning Street), Myrtle, Marion

sheet-15.description: Sheet 15 covers a residential district of north Bridgeton on the east bank of the Cohansey River, the blocks numbered 206, 207 and 208 between North Street on the north and Laning Street on the south. Cohansey Street runs the length of the sheet and divides the two main blocks; Nichols Street bounds the western block along its low, curving west side, with a strip of lots between it and the Central Railroad of New Jersey (the wide bundle of tracks marked no exposure) and marsh land at the lower left. North Laurel Street forms the east side of the sheet, and Myrtle Street enters it from the east near the lower right. A small street, Mount Vernon Street, and Grant Street come in from the north above North Street, where the sheet shows the corner of block 32 and part of the district to the north-east along North Street. The buildings are almost entirely detached frame dwellings, most with a rear auto house or shed; the 1st Methodist Protestant Church, with its tower, stands on the east side of Cohansey Street, and there is a private garage near the lower right corner. Six inch water pipes run in North, Cohansey, Laning and Nichols Streets and a fourteen inch main in North Laurel Street. The map is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and is turned so that north points up and to the left (the compass rose is at the upper left). The blocks across Laning Street at the bottom and across North Laurel Street are drawn on sheets 14, 16 and 18.
notes: Laning Street is Lanning Street in OpenStreetMap.
Nichols Street is drawn about 90 m east of the modern Nichols Street line, so Nichols was left out of the control.
Fitted scale about 2 percent larger than the atlas scan constant.
map, 50 ft: N. Pearl / N. Laurel / Cohansey blocks; Nichols St left out (modern line about 90 m west)

sheet-16.description: Sheet 16 covers a residential district of north-central Bridgeton, in the blocks numbered 108, 109, 111 and 112 on either side of Myrtle Street. The upper half shows two long blocks between North Laurel Street on the left, North Pearl Street in the middle and Bank Street to the right, with a third narrow row of lots between North Pearl and Bank; the east side of the sheet is bounded by the line of Walnut Street. Myrtle Street crosses the middle of the sheet, and below it the lower half shows the blocks between North Pearl Street, Bank Street and Walnut Street, cut diagonally by Irving Avenue, which runs from the lower left towards the right edge. Myrtle Terrace is a short lane opening off the south side of Myrtle Street on the left, and Rose Street enters from the left near the lower left. Housing is nearly all detached frame dwellings with small auto houses. The commercial and industrial buildings are concentrated near Myrtle Street: a bakery of brick with a gas oven and fire proof box on the north side at North Pearl, the Edmund A. Loper milk and ice cream premises on the south side, a repair shop and garage with coloured fill south of Myrtle between North Pearl and Bank, and an apartment building near Irving Avenue. A large block on the left is left blank, being drawn on sheet 14. Six and fourteen inch water pipes are marked in the main streets. The map is drawn at 50 feet to an inch, turned so that north lies up and to the left, with the compass at the lower left. Adjoining sheets are 15 at the left, 18 above, 17 at the right and 12 and 14 below.
notes: Printed street names are N. Laurel, N. Pearl, Bank, Walnut and Myrtle without a suffix; modern names are North Laurel Street, North Pearl Street, Bank Street, Walnut Street and Myrtle Street.
Myrtle Terrace is not in OpenStreetMap.
map, 50 ft

sheet-17.description: Sheet 17 covers the north-eastern edge of central Bridgeton, where a wide railroad corridor cuts diagonally across the sheet from the lower left to the upper right. West of the corridor a single long block, number 113, runs between Bank Street and Walnut Street from Orchard Street at the top down to Myrtle Street, filled with detached frame dwellings with small auto houses; the Model Laundry, with a pink-filled brick building, stands about two thirds of the way down. The railroad lines are drawn as bundles of thin tracks, with three spurs on wood trestles at the lower left and a storage building beside them. East of the corridor the sheet shows blocks 388, 389 and 118: a row of narrow lots fronting Lakeview Avenue at the right edge, an open triangle with a few houses off Hobson Street, E. Myrtle Street crossing the middle, and a long row of well-built dwellings on the north side of Irving Avenue, which runs along the bottom of the sheet. The cross streets Church Street, North East Avenue and Yorke Street come up to Irving Avenue from the south, where the area is drawn on sheets 12, 13 and 35. A short stretch of Orchard Street appears again at the upper right. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and is rotated slightly clockwise, with the compass rose at the upper left; the lower left and upper left margins are left blank, being drawn on adjoining sheets 16, 18 and 19. Six inch water pipes run in most streets.
notes: Printed E. Myrtle is East Myrtle Street today; Yorke Street is York Street in OpenStreetMap; North East Avenue is East Avenue.
The Orchard Street at the upper left, between Bank and Walnut, is Seibel Street in OpenStreetMap and was matched to it; the Orchard Street at the upper right is West Orchard Street.
East Avenue and York Street are not drawn north of Irving Avenue.
map, 50 ft: turned about +5 deg unlike its neighbours; rail corridor through the middle; Orchard = Seibel Street

sheet-18.description: Sheet 18 covers a residential and institutional district of northern Bridgeton, in the blocks numbered 111, 112, 204, 205 and 211. The sheet is turned about 33 degrees, with the compass rose at the upper left, so that North Pearl Street and Bank Street run down the right half and North Street climbs diagonally from the lower left. North Laurel Street forms the lower left edge, Charles Street crosses the upper left, and Harrison Street runs down the middle between a long block of narrow frame dwellings and the open ground of Markley Drive, a curving private drive that serves an apartment house and a few houses on large lots at the left. Morton Street is lettered along the top edge. Orchard Street crosses the lower right, between North Pearl and Bank Streets. The sheet's institutions stand along these streets: the Immaculate Conception R. C. School, in pink, at the top; the Immaculate Conception R. C. Church, with its tower, and the convent, lyceum and rectory beside North Street; and the Pearl St. Public School, a large pink-filled brick building with a stairway tower, below Orchard Street at the lower right. A garage for thirty cars stands on Bank Street, and an auto repair shop on Harrison Street. Water pipes of six inches run in most streets. The map is drawn at 50 feet to an inch. Block 33 at the top left and block 34 at the top right belong to sheets 33 and 34; sheets 15, 16, 17, 19 and 32 adjoin.
notes: The Orchard Street between North Pearl and Bank Streets is Seibel Street in OpenStreetMap and was matched to it.
The junction of Charles Street and Harrison Street was left out of the fit as it lay about 3 m off the others.
Printed N. Pearl and N. Laurel are North Pearl Street and North Laurel Street today.
map, 50 ft: Charles / Harrison junction left out; Orchard = Seibel Street

sheet-19-1.description: Sheet 19, part 1, is the left part of the sheet, the area west of the heavy vertical dividing line, and shows an industrial strip of northern Bridgeton between Bank Street and the railroad. Bank Street runs the full height of the sheet at the left, with Orchard Street along the bottom edge. The strip between them is occupied by the works of the Hamper and Basket Manufacturing Company: five long frame and asbestos-clad warehouses and the saw mill (numbered 1 to 8 on the plan), long basket sheds, a boiler or steam plant, a water tank in a small square enclosure, an office and several outbuildings, with railroad sidings curving in from the right and serving them. A large block of buildings, partly blue and partly brown filled, stands at the top, and below the basket company the sheet shows Joseph Toye Brass and Iron Castings, with a foundry in pink, a grinding shed and a sand and coke house, and at the lower end the large pink-filled Greenebaum Bros and Co. shirt factory. To the right of the works the sheet shows a bundle of railroad tracks running north-east with a broad curving line and an open area numbered 35. Orchard Street and Lakeview Avenue appear in the lower right of the part as lettered streets with no buildings. The part is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned about 33 degrees, with its own compass rose; the right part of the sheet, on the other side of the heavy line, is a separate map of Tumbling Dam Park. Blocks 18, 34 and 17 on the margins are on adjoining sheets.
notes: The Orchard at the lower left, meeting Bank Street, is Seibel Street in OpenStreetMap.
Anchored on one point (Bank Street and Seibel Street) with the atlas scale and the rotation from its measured lines: low confidence.
map, 50 ft, 2 parts split by a vertical heavy line: 1 left (Bank St, Hamper & Basket Mfg Co, railroad; anchored on Bank / Orchard = Seibel); 2 right (Tumbling Dam Park, Sunset Lake; unplaced)

Not georeferenced on this sheet: right of the heavy line: Tumbling Dam Park and Sunset Lake (no street junction (Rammells Mill Road not in OpenStreetMap); needs step 6b carried points from sheet 37-2 (Park Drive = Mayor Aitken Drive) or parcel corners).

sheet-20.description: Sheet 20 covers the north-west edge of Bridgeton along the Cohansey River, where the city runs out into Jeddy's Pond and the park. The map is turned about 18 degrees, with the compass rose at the left. The sheet is crossed from the upper left to the lower right by the mill raceway of the Bridgeton Pleasure Boat Company, a broad channel lined with boat houses, which joins the river near Park Drive. Park Drive runs down the right of the centre from the Bridgeton Water Works pumping station, a group of pink and brown brick buildings with filter house, pump house, boiler house and coal pile, with settling basins to its left, to West Commerce Street at the bottom. City Park occupies the open ground between Park Drive and the river, with a few small buildings and a pavilion-like structure; Ivy Hall Sanitarium and the B. P. O. E. lodge stand near West Commerce Street, and a pants factory lies at the lower right beside East Commerce Street and the bridge over the river. On the left are the residential streets: Franklin Drive running north-west from Lake Street to a turning loop at the top, North Franklin Street running south to West Commerce Street, and the curving inner Franklin Drive that bounds a few large houses and a tile house on their grounds. Washington Street is lettered at the right edge. Streets run at six and sixteen inch pipe, and a large block of 29 at the lower left is blank, belonging to sheet 29. The map is drawn at 50 feet to an inch; sheet 21 adjoins below and 8 and 2 at the right.
notes: Park Drive is Mayor Aitken Drive in OpenStreetMap; North Franklin Street south of Lake Street is Franklin Drive there, and the Franklin Drive printed at the upper left continues it north-west.
The inner curving street lettered Franklin Drive is not in OpenStreetMap.
Fitted with three control points only (exact fit, no leave-one-out): low confidence.
Fitted scale about 2.5 percent smaller than the atlas scan constant.
map, 50 ft: Park Drive (Mayor Aitken Drive), N. Franklin, W. Commerce, water works; three-point fit

sheet-21.description: Sheet 21 covers the commercial core of Bridgeton on the west bank of the Cohansey River, between West Commerce Street at the top and Atlantic Terrace near the bottom, with the river running down the right-hand side. Atlantic Street runs the length of the sheet, and Broad Street crosses it about halfway down, continuing east towards the river as Jefferson Street. North of Broad the blocks hold a mix of dwellings and trades: a hardware store, a plumbing shop, a machine shop, an auto washing and storage building, an auto trucks and tractor storage shed, warerooms for farm implements, tractor and auto repair shops, the Bridgeton Textile Co., a club house and a hotel. East of Atlantic Street, between the street and the river, stand the large pink brick buildings of The M. C. Schrank Co., makers of undergarments, with a garment factory and a small lumber pile behind, and the Bridgeton Business School. South of Broad Street the sheet shows the Cumberland County Court House and the County Jail at the left, H. H. Hankins & Bros. lumber yard and sawing and planing mill, and on the riverfront Serata & Sons, a feed mill and a hay, feed and fertilizer warehouse, with Newell's Lane, Water Street and the works of The Bridgeton Gas Light Co. and an oxide house towards the bottom right. A railroad siding runs along the river at the lower right. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch, with a north arrow turned about 20 degrees to the left of the page. Sheets 20, 29, 23, 24, 22, 2 and 4 are indicated as adjoining at the margins; the east side of the river is left to sheets 2 and 4.
notes: Printed street lettering omits the street type on West Commerce, South Franklin, Broad, Fayette and Water; modern OpenStreetMap names are West Commerce Street, Franklin Street, West Broad Street, Fayette Street and Water Street.
Jefferson Street is drawn as the eastern continuation of Broad Street across the river and is today East Broad Street.
Atlantic Terrace and Newell's Lane are not in the modern OpenStreetMap street data used for the fit.
An Iron Draw Bridge is lettered where West Commerce Street crosses the river at the top of the sheet.
The drawn scale bar reads 50 feet to an inch, and the fitted scale agrees to within about 3 percent.
map, 50 ft: commercial core west of the Cohansey: Atlantic St, Broad, W./E. Commerce, courthouse

sheet-22.description: Sheet 22 is a purely residential sheet in the west of Bridgeton, a grid of six blocks laid out around the crossing of South Giles Street, running down the middle of the sheet, and Hampton Street, which crosses it about halfway down. Vine Street bounds the top row of blocks, Columbus Avenue the left edge, Taylor Street the right edge and New Street the bottom row, and a short Hampton Terrace branches into the block west of South Giles Street. Nearly every lot carries a detached frame dwelling, mostly two storeys, with a small outbuilding at the rear marked auto house or shed; the lots are narrow and deep, and many of the dwellings are paired. The Nazarene Church at 182, at the top left corner on Vine Street, is the only church on the sheet and is lettered as heated by stove and lit by electricity. A junk yard occupies the left side of the block between Hampton and New Streets, and a lumber shed stands within the block on the right of the middle row. Six inch water pipes are shown in Vine, Hampton, Columbus, South Giles and Taylor Streets and a four inch pipe in New Street, with a fire alarm box at Hampton and South Giles. The drawing is at 50 feet to an inch, with the north arrow turned about 20 degrees to the left of the page. Block numbers 231, 232, 234, 235, 316 and 317 are lettered, and the neighbouring sheets are indicated as 29, 28, 23 and 26.
notes: Printed lettering on Vine, Hampton, New and Taylor gives the name only, with no street type; modern OpenStreetMap names are Vine Street, Hampton Street, New Street and Taylor Street.
South Giles is South Giles Street in OpenStreetMap; Columbus Avenue keeps its name.
Hampton Terrace is not in the OpenStreetMap street data used for the fit.
The fitted scale and rotation agree with sheets 21 and 23 to within a few percent and about half a degree.
map, 50 ft: Columbus Av, S. Giles, Taylor, Vine, Hampton, New

sheet-23.description: Sheet 23 shows two groups of blocks in the western part of Bridgeton, either side of Fayette Street, with Vine Street crossing the middle of the sheet and Hampton Street along the bottom. The upper right group lies between Atlantic Terrace at the top and Vine Street, bounded by Fayette Street and Atlantic Street, and holds detached dwellings with a few barns and stables, some set in large lots, plus a pair of small blocks of paired houses at the lower edge. The lower groups lie between Vine and Hampton Streets: to the left of Fayette Street the blocks between Taylor Street and Fayette Street are filled with frame dwellings and outbuildings in narrow lots, and between Fayette Street and Atlantic Street stands the Berean Baptist Temple, a large pink brick church with a fifty foot tower and a thirty seven foot tower at its corner, heated by furnace and lit by gas and electricity. The remainder of that block is dwellings and a poultry operation, a large Poultry Ho with poultry houses and coops around it. A blank rectangle at the upper left, with the number 29 and the north arrow, is another sheet's ground, as are the areas marked 21, 22, 24 and 26. The drawing is at 50 feet to an inch and is turned so that north points about 20 degrees to the left of the top of the page. Six inch water pipes run in Vine, Hampton, Taylor, Fayette and Atlantic Streets and in Atlantic Terrace, and fire hydrants and a fire alarm box mark the corners of the church block.
notes: Atlantic Terrace is not in the OpenStreetMap street data used for the fit; Vine, Hampton, Taylor and Fayette are Vine Street, Hampton Street, Taylor Street and Fayette Street today.
Block numbers 233, 241/2 and 271/2 are lettered on the sheet.
Fit rotation about -19 degrees, as for sheets 21, 22 and 26.
map, 50 ft: Atlantic Ter, Vine, Hampton, Taylor, Fayette, Atlantic St

sheet-24.description: Sheet 24 covers the industrial riverfront strip of Bridgeton on the west bank of the Cohansey River, south of the main business district. Water Street runs down the sheet beside a railroad siding and a freight trestle along the river edge, with Vine Street crossing near the upper third and Hampton Street near the lower third. At the left, Atlantic Street is lined with a row of detached frame dwellings on narrow lots between Vine and Hampton Streets, and State Street is lettered as a short stub off Hampton Street. The centre of the sheet is dominated by the gas works of The Bridgeton Gas Light Co., with its gas holders, coal and coke sheds, shop and storage buildings and a power plant, and by the Star Fish and Bone Fertilizer Co. warehouses to the north-east. Between Vine and Hampton Streets, east of Water Street, are the works of Wm Jerrell and Son, coal and wood, the Wm Lanning and Son canning factory and its numbered warehouses, and The Cox and Sons Co., founders and machinists, whose numbered pattern storage, assembling, machine shop and foundry buildings fill the lower right in pink brick with the traveling crane and pipe shop. West of Water Street the large pink warehouses numbered 7, 8 and 9 belong to Wm Lanning and Son, and a second gas holder of The Bridgeton Gas Light Co. lies to the north and a pattern storage building of The Cox and Sons Co. stands to the south. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch, rotated about 10 degrees to the left of upright. Blank areas lettered 23, 26, 21, 25 and 4 belong to the adjoining sheets, and the right side, across the river, is left to sheet 4.
notes: Printed street names on Atlantic, Vine, Hampton and Water omit the street type; modern OpenStreetMap names are Atlantic Street, Vine Street, Hampton Street and Water Street.
The fit rotation of about -10 degrees differs from the -19 degrees of sheets 21 to 23 and 26; the drawing is turned on this sheet.
Vine Street and Water Street meet in a junction that the fit puts about 3 m from the drawn pipe corner; Water Street may have been realigned.
A railroad siding and a freight trestle are drawn along the river edge.
map, 50 ft: Water St riverfront industry; turned about 10 deg relative to 21-23

sheet-25.description: Sheet 25 shows the industrial and open land at the southern end of the Bridgeton riverfront, between Water Street on the left and the Cohansey River, which curves across the upper right and runs off the sheet at the lower right. Water Street runs down the left side, bending to run straight south, with Lincoln Street entering from the west near the top left. A railroad, with a freight siding, runs down the sheet parallel to Water Street. At the top are the Clinton B. Ayars Canning Co. works, with warehouses, a large canning building and storage, a garage with room for fourteen cars, and a boat house on the river bank. Below them The Crescent Art Metal Co., makers of lighting fixtures, occupies a pink brick plant with polishing, foundry, acid and dipping and lacquering rooms. Further down are the Gulf Refining Co. gasoline and oil station and, along the railroad, a row of numbered iron oil tanks and a cement storage building; the Standard Oil Co. of N.J. has a large lot east of the railroad with a warehouse, pump house, kerosene and gasoline tanks and a numbered group of oil tanks, which the surveyor marked as admittance refused. Lower down are the Sinclair Refining Co. station with gasoline tanks, the Atlantic Refining Co. oil warehouse, and, at the bottom, the Bridgeton Sewage Disposal Plant with its drying beds, Imhoff tanks, pump house, filtration beds and settling basins. Much of the right half is open ground bounded only by lot lines. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch. The numbers 24 and 26 lettered in blank areas mark the adjoining sheets.
notes: Water is lettered without a street type; the modern street is Water Street.

Placed from a single hand-picked junction (Lincoln Street and Water Street, taken at the corner of the drawn water pipes) with the sheet scale and the rotation taken from the modern Water Street, which bends at the same place as the drawn street; low confidence.
Admittance refused is lettered at the Gulf Refining Co. and Standard Oil Co. of N.J. premises, so their interiors are not drawn.
map, 50 ft: Water St south of Lincoln, oil works, sewage plant; placed by one hand-picked point (low confidence)

sheet-26.description: Sheet 26 covers a large residential district in the south-west of Bridgeton, drawn at 100 feet to an inch, so that the blocks and detached dwellings appear small. It is laid out on a regular grid of streets running from Hampton Street at the top to Belmont Avenue at the bottom, with New Street, Lincoln Street, Woodland Drive, Institute Place and Cottage Avenue crossing from west to east. Fayette Street and Atlantic Street run north to south through the middle of the sheet, State Street lies to the east of Atlantic Street, and Oxford Street bounds the lower right. Water Street runs diagonally in the upper right, with Woodland Drive curving round a group of irregular lots beside it. Almost every lot carries a frame dwelling, mostly two storeys, with a small outbuilding at the rear, and the blocks are numbered between 222A and 319B; the numbers 22, 23, 24, 25 and 27 mark the neighbouring sheets. Taylor Street appears as a short stub at the top left. The ground to the east of Water Street is drawn only as lot lines. No factories, churches or schools are shown. Six inch water pipes are marked in most of the streets and four inch pipes in New Street, Lincoln Street and Cottage Avenue. The north arrow is turned about 20 degrees to the left of the page.
notes: Several streets are lettered without a street type; modern OpenStreetMap names are Hampton Street, New Street, Lincoln Street, Fayette Street, Atlantic Street, State Street, Water Street and Oxford Street.
The sheet is drawn at 100 feet to an inch, unlike the neighbouring sheets 21 to 24, which are at 50 feet; the atlas needs scale_ft 100 for this sheet.
Woodland Drive is a curved street between Atlantic Street and Institute Place.
map, 100 ft: residential grid

sheet-27.description: Sheet 27 is drawn at 100 feet to an inch and covers the south-western edge of Bridgeton, mostly thinly built or undeveloped. Fayette Street runs diagonally from the top left to the bottom centre and Atlantic Street runs close to it as a second long street, with Belmont Avenue and Summit Avenue crossing at the top. Below them a fan of streets, University Avenue, Princeton Avenue, Rogers Avenue and Harvard Avenue, runs east from Atlantic Street towards Oxford Street at the right, laid out as long blocks of narrow lots with very few buildings; Oxford Street itself and some other streets are lettered as not open. The top strip holds a few scattered dwellings and poultry sheds between Belmont and Summit Avenues, and in the upper right corner the Bridgeton Chandelier Co. Inc. has an office and storage building, a machine shop, finishing building, storage and foundry, with the block numbered 371. At the left lie the Garden State Fair Grounds: a curved race track and a grand stand, a wooden grand stand, stables and small outbuildings, with a stable 200 feet away marked by an arrow. Near the bottom a pond and the Island Branch Run, marked City Limits where it forms the boundary, cross the sheet beneath the Central Railroad of New Jersey, and a road runs south past a poultry building and a dwelling at the lower left. Water pipes are marked along many of the built streets. The north arrow is turned about 20 degrees to the left of the page. Sheet 26 adjoins at the top, with the numbers 235, 536, 537, 539, 541 and 543 marking neighbouring blocks.
notes: Rogers Avenue is today Rutgers Avenue; Belmont, Summit, University, Princeton and Harvard Avenues keep their names. Atlantic, Fayette and Oxford are lettered without a street type; the modern streets are Atlantic Street, Fayette Street and Oxford Street.
The sheet is drawn at 100 feet to an inch (3.9 px/ft fitted); the atlas needs scale_ft 100 for this sheet.
The fit uses a second-order polynomial; the Oxford Street junctions carry 4 to 5 m residuals and Oxford Street may be displaced from its drawn line.
Several streets east of Atlantic Street are lettered Not Open.
map, 100 ft: south-west edge, fair grounds, Island Branch Run; Rogers Av = Rutgers Avenue

sheet-28-1.description: The main part of sheet 28 covers the south-western edge of built-up Bridgeton west of the Cohansey, drawn at 100 feet to an inch. Vine Street runs across the top of the sheet and Hampton Street and New Street across the middle; Jackson Street, lower down, is built up only between South Lawrence Street and Columbus Avenue. The north-south streets are Cemetery Road on the far left, South West Avenue, South Lawrence Street and Columbus Avenue, and Bowentown Road leaves the upper left corner towards the north-west. The blocks along Hampton Street and Vine Street west of South Lawrence Street are only partly built, with deep vacant lots, while the blocks between South Lawrence Street and Columbus Avenue are filled with rows of frame dwellings, several of them double houses, with auto houses behind. There is no industry on the part. Overlook Cemetery lies beyond Cemetery Road in the lower left, left blank. The lower part of the sheet, below a heavy line, carries two insets of county institutions outside the city: the Cumberland County Alms House and the Cumberland County Hospital for the Insane (parts 2 and 3, not placed).
notes: Jackson Street and Cemetery Road are not in OpenStreetMap under these names; the modern streets laid out south of New Street (Lincoln Street, Suncrest Avenue) do not follow the 1930 lines.

map, 3 parts: main (Vine, Hampton, New, Jackson, West Av, Cemetery Rd, Columbus Av); insets: Cumberland County Alms House (2 mi SW of City Hall) and Cumberland County Hospital for the Insane (1.5 mi SW)

Not georeferenced on this sheet: inset: The Cumberland County Alms House, located 2 miles SW of City Hall (no street junction; outside the reference box; needs parcel or building match with a reference box extended about 3 km south-west).

Not georeferenced on this sheet: inset: The Cumberland County Hospital for the Insane, located 1.5 miles SW of City Hall (no street junction; outside the reference box; needs parcel or building match with a reference box extended about 3 km south-west).

sheet-29.description: Sheet 29 covers a district of Bridgeton west of the centre, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned about 20 degrees on the page. Lake Street crosses near the top, with a row of deep lots running north from it to Jeddys Pond, which curves across the upper left of the sheet; the Lakeview Hospital and a few large dwellings stand on that side, and Franklin Drive leaves the upper right corner towards the north-west. Below Lake Street the sheet is divided into blocks by West Commerce Street, Oak Street, Broad Street, Academy Street and Vine Street, running across the page, and by North and South Lawrence Street on the left, North and South Giles Street in the middle and North and South Franklin Street on the right, running down it. The blocks are numbered 223, 224, 227, 228, 229, 230, 231 1/2 A, 231 1/2 B and 241/3. The drawing is mostly detached frame dwellings with small outbuildings. Institutions include the West Presbyterian Church and its manse on North Giles Street, St. Johns Lutheran Church, Miss Prebels Private School, Trinity M. E. Church, Mt. Zion A. M. E. Church and, at the bottom, the Vine Street Public School, with a bakery beside it. Monumental works stand on the left of the Broad Street block. Powel's Lane runs down a block between Broad and Academy, Bergen Street is a short cross street at lower left, and Atlantic Terrace and Fayette Street appear at the right edge. Four inch to sixteen inch water pipes are drawn in the streets. The margins carry the neighbouring sheet numbers 20, 21, 22, 23, 28 and 30.
notes: The drawn scale is 100 feet to an inch, as the printed scale bar says; atlas.json should carry scale_ft 100 for this sheet.

Broad Street here is West Broad Street in OpenStreetMap; West Commerce Street, Franklin Street, Oak Street and the other streets keep their printed names, with Franklin Street carrying no North or South prefix in the modern data.
The label on the right edge reads Franklin Drive where OpenStreetMap has Franklin Drive.
map, 100 ft

sheet-30-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 30 is the larger area east of the heavy line that runs down the sheet from the upper left to the bottom edge, in the western part of Bridgeton, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned about 20 degrees on the page. West Commerce Street crosses the middle of the upper half, from the triangle where it meets West Avenue to North Lawrence Street at the right edge, with Sherman Street and the short North Lake street running north from it towards a winding creek, Barrett's Run, which flows into Jeddy's Pond at the upper right. South West Avenue runs down the sheet beside the heavy line, and North West Avenue appears in the same strip at the top, where Marlyn Street and the extension of West Commerce Street meet it, crossed by a branch of the Central Railroad of New Jersey. Broad Street crosses at about two thirds of the height and Vine Street along the bottom, with Shiloh Road and Central Avenue as short streets off South West Avenue. South Lawrence Street runs down the right margin, crossed by Oak, Academy and Bergen Streets. Most of the area is a large open block holding the Bridgeton Junior High School, a brick building labelled as built from plans in 1930 with temporary annexes, and the Old Broad Street Presbyterian Church, marked not in use. Houses stand along the north side of West Commerce Street and in blocks 305 and 505. Block numbers 306 and 364 appear. Six, eight and ten inch water pipes are marked. The margins name sheets 28, 29, 30 and 31.
notes: The sheet is cut in two by a heavy line; the area on the other side is part 2. Both parts draw North West Avenue, part 2 at a different place on the page.
The sheet is drawn at 100 feet to an inch, as its scale bar says; the same pond is Jeddys Pond on sheet 29.
Powell Lane, Academy Street and Columbus Avenue in OpenStreetMap lie beyond this part's right edge on sheet 29.
Lawrence Street on the right edge is South Lawrence Street in OpenStreetMap below West Commerce Street and North Lawrence Street above it.

The abbreviations for Shiloh Road and the West Commerce Street extension (printed Shiloh R'd and W. Commerce St. Ext'n N.) are written out here; the reading of North Lake and Barrett's Run is from a reduced view and is medium confidence.
map, 100 ft, 2 parts either side of a heavy line: 1 east (W. Commerce, Lake, Broad, N. Lawrence), 2 west (Preston, Albertson, Burt, Marlyn along N. West Av)

sheet-30-2.description: Part 2 of sheet 30 is the area west of the heavy line that runs down the sheet from the upper left corner to the bottom edge, drawn at 100 feet to an inch. It shows North West Avenue running diagonally down the sheet beside the heavy line, 60 feet wide in places and labelled 66 feet in others, with a series of streets leaving it to the west at a steep angle: Preston Avenue near the top, Albertson Avenue, Burt Avenue, Marlyn Street and, at the bottom of the sheet, the extension of West Commerce Street. Budd Street runs across the lower left between Albertson and Burt Avenues. The blocks are numbered 501, 502, 503, 504, 353 and 354, and are mostly long narrow lots laid out between the streets, many of them vacant. Houses with outbuildings stand along the east side of the area facing North West Avenue and along the south side of West Commerce Street Extension, and a row of hen houses is drawn at the upper left corner and another beside the block 502. A contractor's supply yard stands on the avenue below Burt Avenue. A compass rose stands against the heavy line in the middle of the sheet, pointing north up the page. Water pipes of four, six and eight inches are marked in the streets. The area beyond the heavy line is drawn as part 1 of the same sheet, which also shows North West Avenue.
notes: The sheet is cut in two by a heavy line; the area on the other side is part 1. North West Avenue is drawn in both parts, at different places on the page.
Only four control points were found, all along or near North West Avenue and Budd Street; the rotation (about -16 degrees) differs from part 1 (about -20.5) and is low confidence.
Burt Avenue is Burt Street in OpenStreetMap.
The lettering of Preston Avenue and West Commerce Street Extension was read on reduced crops and is medium confidence.
map, 100 ft, 2 parts either side of a heavy line: 1 east (W. Commerce, Lake, Broad, N. Lawrence), 2 west (Preston, Albertson, Burt, Marlyn along N. West Av)

sheet-31.description: Sheet 31 covers the south-western edge of Bridgeton, where West Commerce Street extension, South West Avenue and Shiloh Road lead out of the built-up area. It is drawn at 100 feet to an inch with north roughly up the page. North and South West Avenue run down the right edge, West Commerce Street Extension crosses the top, and Shiloh Road runs diagonally from the upper left across the sheet to meet Broad Street at the right. Central Avenue crosses the middle from the left edge towards South West Avenue, and Vine Street and Bowentown Road cross the lower half, joining near Cemetery Road at the bottom. Forrest Avenue runs down the lower left. A double-track branch of the Central Railroad of New Jersey cuts diagonally across the sheet from the lower left to the upper right, with a siding, and a stream widens into two ponds beside it. The industrial buildings lie along the railroad: the American Oil Company's Bridgeton bulk station with steel tanks and a pump house, a brick warehouse of the South Jersey Farmers Exchange, Branch No. 12, with a fire plug, and a row of buildings of the Bridgeton Co-operative G.L.F. Service. Houses stand along Shiloh Road, South West Avenue, Forrest Avenue and Bowentown Road. Elsewhere the blocks, numbered 506, 507, 360, 361, 362, 391, 508 and 540, are mostly large undeveloped lots. A dash-dot line crosses the sheet from top to bottom at the left. The margins name sheets 28 and 30.
notes: The sheet is drawn at 100 feet to an inch, as the scale bar says.
Shiloh Road is Shiloh Pike in OpenStreetMap, but the modern Shiloh Pike junction with West Broad Street lies about 900 m west, so Shiloh Road was left out of the control.
Cemetery Road is not in the OpenStreetMap extract.
Broad Street ends here at South West Avenue; it is West Broad Street in OpenStreetMap.
Rotation fits at about -1.6 degrees, against about -20.5 for the neighbouring part of sheet 30 east of its heavy line.
The abbreviations printed as W. Commerce St. Ext'n are written out here; the reading rests on reduced crops and is medium confidence for the Extension suffix.
map, 100 ft: rotation about -2 deg

sheet-32-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 32 is the larger area east of the heavy vertical line, in the north-eastern part of Bridgeton. It is drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned about 85 degrees, so that Irving Avenue runs down the right side of the page and the cross streets run across it. From the top they are Burlington Avenue (Road), Ewing Avenue, Rogers Avenue, Cedarbrook Avenue, Spring Avenue and, at the bottom, Coral Avenue, each 50 to 60 feet wide, with Orchard running down the middle of the part and Dare Avenue meeting Irving Avenue at the lower right. The blocks, numbered 344 to 350 and 515 to 519, are drawn almost entirely as unbuilt lots: long strips of narrow lots laid out along the streets, with only scattered detached frame dwellings and sheds, most of them facing Irving Avenue and Coral Avenue. A florist's range of long greenhouses, labelled T. E. Edwards, Florist, stands on the east side of Irving Avenue, and a pond lies beyond the right edge at the middle of the part. A band shop is marked on Rogers Avenue. Four and six inch water pipes run in the streets. The area to the west of the heavy line is drawn as part 2, and the margins name the neighbouring sheets 33, 35 and 18.
notes: The sheet is drawn at 100 feet to an inch, as the scale bar says, and this part is turned about 85 degrees on the page, with north to the left; part 2 is turned only about 8 degrees.

Avenue names here are Street in OpenStreetMap: Ewing Street, Spring Street; Orchard (the street running down the page) is East Orchard Street, continuing as Orchard Street south of Coral Avenue; Burlington Avenue (Road) is North Burlington Road.
The lettering of Dare Avenue and Orchard Street was read on reduced crops and is medium confidence.
map, 100 ft, 2 parts split by a vertical heavy line: 1 east turned about 85 deg (Burlington Av, Ewing, Rogers, Cedarbrook, Spring, Orchard, Irving), 2 west (Owens-Illinois Glass Co plant, N. Laurel)

sheet-32-2.description: Part 2 of sheet 32 is the narrower area west of the heavy vertical line, in the north-western part of Bridgeton, drawn at 100 feet to an inch with north roughly up the page. It is dominated by the Owens-Illinois Glass Company's Plant 14, a large bottle works with a steel-framed warehouse, lehr building, machine building, furnace building, tanks and a gas producer building, with numbered bottle storage warehouses, storage sheds, a maintenance and repair shop, a blacksmith shop, a mould storage building, an electric shop, auto truck sheds and a general office along North Laurel Street. Above the plant are a paper carton manufactory, paper storage and a paper warehouse, a wooden box factory, a saw and planing mill, a lumber pile and a boiler house marked not in use. The Central Railroad of New Jersey runs down the left side in several tracks, with sidings serving the plant, and two oil tanks are drawn at the left margin. North Laurel Street runs down the middle, crossed by Clark Street, Penn Street, Chestnut Street, German Street and Charles Street. At the lower left a small district of houses lies along Charles Street, Mt. Vernon, Grant and Cohansey Streets and a road, above North Street and Nichols Street, in blocks numbered 53 A and 53 B. A note on the left gives night watchmen's clocks, hose and fire pump arrangements for the plant. The margins name sheets 33, 15, 18 and 35.
notes: The sheet is cut in two by a heavy vertical line; the area on the other side is part 1, turned about 85 degrees.
Four control points were found, three of them on North Laurel Street, so the rotation (about -7.8 degrees) is medium confidence.

The modern Penn Street, Chestnut Avenue and North Laurel Street meet at one junction; Charles is Charles Street, Mt. Vernon is Mount Vernon Street, and North is North Street in OpenStreetMap. Grant and German Street were not found in OpenStreetMap by those names.
The drawn railroad lies about 15 m from the modern Bridgeton Port Branch line, along the track.
The street printed only as Road at the lower left has no name before it on the sheet and its modern name was not identified; the reading is low confidence.
The abbreviation Mt. is written out as Mount.
map, 100 ft, 2 parts split by a vertical heavy line: 1 east turned about 85 deg (Burlington Av, Ewing, Rogers, Cedarbrook, Spring, Orchard, Irving), 2 west (Owens-Illinois Glass Co plant, N. Laurel)

sheet-33-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 33 is the main map, covering a residential and part-open district in the north-west of Bridgeton between North Laurel Street on the left and North Pearl Street, which cuts diagonally up the right side. It is drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned about 7 degrees. Bridgeton Avenue forms the top edge, with houses and coops along it, and Cumberland, German, Monroe, Madison and Penn Streets cross the sheet, with Charles Street at the bottom. Chestnut Street runs from the top down to meet North Laurel Street at lower left, High Street runs down the middle, and Bank Street, Morton Street and Harrison Street lead off the lower right. Most of the area is closely built with detached frame dwellings, with larger open blocks numbered 213, 301 and 341 in the upper half and a cemetery in the lower middle. Institutions are the Monroe Street Public School, the North Pearl Street Baptist Church, the Wesley Memorial M. E. Church and a garage and car storage building on North Pearl Street, and an auto grave yard is marked in block 213. A greenhouse stands beside Madison Street. Several blocks at the left edge are shown as isolated houses on a road west of North Laurel Street, with Clark Street entering at the left. The sheet carries block numbers from 201 to 216, 301, 336 to 341, 385 to 387, and the lower right is cut off by the heavy line enclosing part 2. Water pipes of four to fourteen inches are marked, and a railroad crosses at the upper left corner.
notes: The heavy line at the lower right encloses part 2, which draws Highland Avenue, North Pearl Street and Edward Avenue at a similar scale and rotation.
German Street is American Avenue in OpenStreetMap; Cumberland is Cumberland Avenue, Monroe is Monroe Street, Chestnut is Chestnut Avenue, and North Laurel is North Laurel Street.
The rotation is about -7.5 degrees; the fitted scale is about 4 percent above the printed 100 feet to an inch and 2 percent above the other 100 foot sheets.
The street at the left edge is printed only as Road, with no name before it.
map, 100 ft, 2 parts: 1 main (Bridgeton Av, Cumberland, German = American Avenue, Monroe, Madison, Penn); 2 lower right inside the heavy line (Highland Av, N. Pearl, Edward Av; three points)

sheet-33-2.description: Part 2 of sheet 33 is the area at the lower right inside the heavy line, in the north of Bridgeton, drawn at 100 feet to an inch. It shows the angle between three streets running together: North Pearl Street, which runs diagonally up the right side of the part, Highland Avenue, which joins it from the upper left, and Edward Avenue, which runs down the left side from the upper left to Bridgeton Avenue at the bottom. Rosenhayn Road leaves North Pearl Street to the right near the bottom edge, where Bridgeton Avenue crosses. The built-up land is a strip of detached frame houses with sheds, coops and an auto-repair or store building along the west side of North Pearl Street, numbered in the 650s to 690s, and a few houses on Highland Avenue; blocks 338 and 336 hold large undrawn lots, and the rest of the part, including a triangular block numbered 500, is blank. Six inch water pipes run in Edward Avenue, North Pearl Street and Bridgeton Avenue. The sheet number 34 stands beside the part, which borders the main part of the sheet along the heavy line.
notes: Only three control points were found, one of them hand-picked at Highland Avenue and North Pearl Street (the detector's own reading of that junction was 16 m off), so the placement is an exact three-point fit and is low confidence; scale (about 3.99 pixels per foot) and rotation (about -8 degrees) agree with part 1.
Rosenhayn Road is Rosenhayn Avenue in OpenStreetMap, and North Pearl is North Pearl Street.
The part is taken to be the area inside the heavy line at the lower right, bounded by the diagonal line from near the compass rose and the vertical line at its left.
map, 100 ft, 2 parts: 1 main (Bridgeton Av, Cumberland, German = American Avenue, Monroe, Madison, Penn); 2 lower right inside the heavy line (Highland Av, N. Pearl, Edward Av; three points)

sheet-34-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 34 is the wider area west of the heavy vertical line, along the north side of Bridgeton, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned about 33 degrees. North Pearl Street runs down the left side of the part, built up on its west side with scattered houses, sheds, auto repair shops and filling stations (auto repair buildings appear near the top) and with a long run of narrow lots behind it, numbered in blocks 338, 339 and 500. At the bottom left, North Pearl Street meets Bridgeton Avenue, Edward Avenue and the diagonal Rosenhayn Road, which runs up the page to the right, past a sheet metal shop and the plant of Fred Michelbach, manufacturer of concrete products. Highland Avenue enters at the left edge higher up. The centre of the part is a wide band of railroad right-of-way, the West Jersey and Seashore Railroad (marked D. R. R.) and the Central Railroad of New Jersey, with a siding. Beside it stand large industrial works: the Eastern Plate and Window Glass Company, with a furnace and warehouse, and the Salem Brass and Iron Manufacturing Company's foundry, labelled with its watchman's clock, fire protection and heating notes. Block numbers 340 and 342 are marked, and Bank Street meets the bottom edge. The block to the east of the heavy line is drawn as part 2 of the same sheet.
notes: The heavy line cuts the sheet in two; the area on the other side is part 2, which draws North Pearl Street again on a different part of the sheet.

This part is placed from three points: Bridgeton Avenue with North Pearl Street and Rosenhayn Road, and Bridgeton Avenue with Edward Avenue (both hand-picked), with scale and rotation taken from part 2 (3.995 pixels per foot, -33.3 degrees); Highland Avenue with North Pearl Street fell about 70 pixels from where that placement puts it. Low confidence.
Rosenhayn Road is Rosenhayn Avenue in OpenStreetMap, and North Pearl is North Pearl Street.
The sheet's scale bar says 100 feet to an inch; atlas.json should carry scale_ft 100 for sheet 34.
map, 100 ft, 2 parts split by a vertical heavy line: 1 west (N. Pearl, Rosenhayn Av; anchored on two hand picks), 2 east (N. Pearl, Bank, Cumberland, Horton, Penn)

sheet-34-2.description: Part 2 of sheet 34 is the area east of the heavy vertical line, in the north of Bridgeton, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned about 33 degrees. North Pearl Street runs down the left side and Bank Street down the right, crossed from the top by Cumberland Street, German Street, Monroe Street, Horton Street, Madison Street, Penn Street and, at the bottom, Morton Street; Bank Street splits off diagonally across the upper half. Blocks numbered 43, 44, 45, 211, 217, 302 and 512 hold close rows of detached frame houses, mostly along North Pearl Street, with larger industrial works on the right. These are the Owens-Illinois Glass Company, formerly the More Jonas plant, with bottle and storage warehouses, a furnace house and an office; the American Can Company, makers of tin cans, a large sprinklered complex with a vacant warehouse beside it belonging to Chas. F. Dare and Son; the Fairdale Canning Company with its cannery and warehouse; Menz Bros. and Smith cleaning and dyeing; and Loder's coal yard at the top. Auto sales and service stations stand on Penn Street. Railroad tracks of the Central Railroad of New Jersey and the West Jersey and Seashore Railroad run in a bundle down the right side, with the unopened Railroad Avenue at lower right. The area to the west of the heavy line is part 1. Sheet numbers 18, 19, 33 and 35 are named in the margins.
notes: The heavy line cuts the sheet in two; the area on the other side is part 1.
German Street is American Avenue in OpenStreetMap; Cumberland Street is Cumberland Avenue; North Pearl is North Pearl Street.
Railroad Avenue is lettered Not Opened on the sheet.
The sheet's scale bar says 100 feet to an inch; atlas.json should carry scale_ft 100 for sheet 34.
The Penn Street crossing of the railroad was rejected as 14 m from the fit, so the railroad control was not used.
map, 100 ft, 2 parts split by a vertical heavy line: 1 west (N. Pearl, Rosenhayn Av; anchored on two hand picks), 2 east (N. Pearl, Bank, Cumberland, Horton, Penn)

sheet-35.description: Sheet 35 covers the north-eastern edge of Bridgeton at 100 feet to an inch, with north roughly at the top. Indian Avenue forms the top edge, and Holly Street and Orchard Street cross the sheet from west to east, with Railroad, Magnolia, Manheim and Coral Avenues running down it, their blocks numbered in the 300s (329 to 333, 343, 344, 514). The built-up part is the upper right, a district of detached frame dwellings on long narrow lots, with coops, sheds and an auto repair shop. Bridgeton Hospital stands near the middle, a fireproof brick building with nurses' quarters, and the Irving Avenue Presbyterian Church lies beside it. Irving Avenue itself runs diagonally from the middle to the lower left, with the Irving Avenue Public School, a railroad station of the same name, and small houses along it. Albert Atkinson, florist, has long greenhouses to the right of Manheim Avenue. Railroad tracks of the Central Railroad of New Jersey run down the middle of the sheet, with the West Jersey and Seashore Railroad curving through a large open tract at the upper left, and Indian Field Run, a stream, crosses the lower right. Nixon Avenue, Lakeview Avenue, East Myrtle Street and Yorke Street lie at the left, where large blocks (303, 104, 120) are mostly unbuilt. Water pipes of four and six inches run in the streets. The margins give neighbouring sheets 13, 17, 19, 32, 34 and 36.
notes: The sheet is drawn at 100 feet to an inch, as the scale bar says; atlas.json should carry scale_ft 100 for sheet 35 (the lead's notes did not list it).
Yorke is York Street in OpenStreetMap; Indian is Indian Avenue, Holly is Holly Street, Orchard is Orchard Street (West Orchard Street west of Railroad Avenue).

Three junctions along Coral Avenue (with Orchard Street, Indian Avenue and Irving Avenue) and the Irving Avenue and Manheim Avenue junction were 13 to 17 m from the fit and were left out as outliers, probably because modern Coral Avenue and Irving Avenue are not on their 1930 lines.
Railroad Avenue is lettered Not Opened above Holly Street.
Penn is read from the diagonal street at the top left on a reduced crop and is medium confidence.
map, 100 ft

sheet-36.description: Sheet 36 covers the south-eastern edge of Bridgeton around the Ferracute Machine Company, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned about 14 degrees. East Commerce Street crosses the bottom, with Buckshutem Road leaving it diagonally to the lower right, and Manheim, Coral and Dare Avenues run down the right side as wide strips, partly marked not opened, cut by Gilmore Avenue. Railroad Avenue and Elm run down the left of centre, with Dare Street and Strawberry Street crossing them. The Ferracute Machine Company's works fill the lower left: a large machine shop, a pattern shop, a pattern storage building and a foundry, with a long spur from the railroad serving them, and the Crystal Ice and Cold Storage Company's ice store and freezing trunks stand at the top of the same strip. The Herman Z. Cutler Company, sheet metal works, stamps and dies, has a machine shop beside the tracks of the Central Railroad of New Jersey and of the West Jersey and Seashore branch, which run down the middle of the sheet. A winding creek, Indian Field Run, enters at the top left and a river or pond edge runs down the left side, where the estate Lochwold stands with a boat house. Small blocks of dwellings stand along East Commerce Street, Strawberry Street and Gilmore Avenue, a public school and a church appear on the right, and a garage and a bottled soft drink storage building stand beside East Commerce Street. The blocks are numbered in the 100s, 300s and 400s (104 A to 104 C, 327, 350, 355, 377, 384, 385). The margins name sheets 35, 37, 38, 40 and 41.
notes: The sheet is drawn at 100 feet to an inch, as the scale bar says, and is turned about 14 degrees (north towards the upper left).

Gilmore Avenue is Gilmore Street in OpenStreetMap; East Commerce Street is Commerce Street East east of the Railroad; Elm is North Elm Street; Strawberry is Strawberry Street; Dare Avenue and Dare Street keep their names.
Manheim, Coral and Dare Avenues are drawn as wide strips and carry the label Not Opened above Gilmore Avenue.
South Railroad Avenue is printed S. Railroad Av. at the bottom edge; Lochwold is printed in quotation marks.
map, 100 ft

sheet-37-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 37 shows the eastern edge of Bridgeton, drawn at 100 feet to an inch, along East Commerce and out the Burlington road. It occupies the lower and right-hand side of the sheet, below and east of the heavy line that separates it from the turned part to the north-west. East Commerce runs across the bottom of the part from left to right, with the fifty-foot Park Avenue meeting it from the north at the left and the Burlington road (marked Avenue (Road)) crossing it at the right, near a gasoline station and a few dwellings and coops. Park Avenue and the unopened Ava Avenue run down from the heavy line towards East Commerce through large undeveloped parcels, several carrying only lot numbers and the name Albert R. Horner beside a dwelling. At the left, Gilmore Avenue (not opened) and Dare Avenue are drawn as outlines of future streets, with a small circular reservoir of 2,490,000 gallons capacity, thirty feet above ground and concrete, and a valve house with sixteen-inch and six-inch water pipes near East Commerce. Lancaster and Luzerne are laid out below East Commerce but not opened. Reeves Road leaves the Burlington road towards the north-east at the top right, with a few dwellings and the Jan. 1930 Bridgeton title stamp above it. Development is sparse: frame dwellings and outbuildings along the Burlington road and East Commerce, and open ground elsewhere. Blank paper at the left edge belongs to sheets 33 and 36, whose numbers are printed on the sheet.
notes: Burlington Road is North Burlington Road and South Burlington Road in OpenStreetMap, meeting East Commerce (Commerce Street East) at the junction used as control.
Gilmore Avenue is Gilmore Street today; Park Avenue and Dare Avenue keep their names. Ava Avenue, Lancaster and Luzerne are not in OpenStreetMap.

sheet-37-2.description: Part 2 of sheet 37 is the north-western piece of the sheet, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned about 38 degrees clockwise from the other part, with its own north arrow pointing up and to the right. It lies above and to the left of the heavy line and shows the northern edge of the city. A sixty-foot North Laurel runs diagonally from the top edge down to the lower left, crossing Stone Bridge Run and a lake that the city line passes through. Park Drive, also called Rammell's Mill Road, runs across the upper left, lined with numbered lots and a row of frame dwellings and outbuildings on its north side. Further down, North Laurel is bordered by long lots with more dwellings and an auto repair shop with a cement floor. At the bottom, Bridgeton Avenue and Chestnut run off at right angles from the heavy line in a narrow triangle that also holds the C.R.R. of N.J. line and a few small buildings. The heavy line carries the sheet number 33 beside Bridgeton Avenue. Most of the area is open ground, with lots numbered 380, 510, 511 and 335, and the note vacant beyond at the top edge. Blank paper at the left belongs to the neighbouring sheet.
notes: North Laurel continues north of Bridgeton Avenue as Old Deerfield Pike in OpenStreetMap; Bridgeton Avenue and Chestnut are Bridgeton Avenue and Chestnut Avenue today; Park Drive keeps its name.

The part has only three control points (two detected, one hand-picked at Park Drive and Old Deerfield Pike), so it is an exact fit with low confidence; the fitted scale is about 4.04 px per foot against the printed 100 feet to an inch.
Railroad crossings were left out of the fit: the crossing of the railroad with Chestnut lies about 10 metres from its modern position.

sheet-38-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 38 is the main map of an area south-east of the city centre, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned about fourteen degrees from north. It is bounded at the top by Mill, with Pine Street at the upper left, and at the bottom by Henry and the diagonal Willow, which cuts across the sheet from the upper left to the lower right. In the upper part, Mill Creek winds across the sheet beside the line of the W.J. & S. R.R. (P.R.R.), and a few dwellings stand on Pine Street and Mill. At the top right the large pink works of the Martin Dyeing and Finishing Co. (dye and finishing buildings, storage and a chemical store) reach to East Commerce. The middle of the sheet holds Terrace, with Edgewood Avenue, Ellis and South East Avenue running south from it and Division on the right. Below Terrace the blocks are mostly empty large parcels numbered 307, 308 and 309, with dwellings strung out along the streets. At the lower left, South Pine and Spruce run south across Henry, lined with frame dwellings and several poultry houses, and a Union Baptist Church and a Baptist Chapel (South) stand on the left. Large lots numbered 310 and 311 fill the bottom right. The box at the right edge, below the dye works, is an inset of its own and is not part of this part. The numbers 5, 6, 7, 36 and 39 at the margins refer to adjoining sheets.
notes: South Pine is South Pine Street or Pine Street South in OpenStreetMap; South East Avenue and Spruce keep their names; East Commerce is East Commerce Street or Commerce Street East.
Willow runs diagonally here but is drawn to match the modern Willow Street; the junctions of Willow with Edgewood Avenue, Ellis, South East Avenue and Division agree with the fit to 1 to 2 metres.

Eight junctions were used (RMSE 1.4 m, leave-one-out 2.9 m, about 3.97 px per foot); hand-picked Terrace and Mill junctions disagreed with the others by 3 to 14 metres and were left out, so the top third of the part has no control of its own.
The inset at the right (Martin Dyeing Co. area, marked 38 and 36) has no street junction and is not georeferenced.

sheet-39.description: Sheet 39 is a single map at 100 feet to an inch of the district south of the city centre, turned about fifteen degrees from north, and drawn with a clay works at the upper right. South Pine and Spruce run from top to bottom through the middle, crossed by Fremont near the top, Garfield in the middle and Pamphylia Avenue near the bottom. On the left South runs beside blocks of frame dwellings, with Grove at the far left and Cedar Dell Avenue below, where the New Jersey Button Works stands on the left side with its stores and sheds. A Church of the Nazarene stands on South, and an automobile painting and trimming shop and a structural iron works stand at the bottom left. On the right, Colfax and South East Avenue bound a large block holding the Erickson Brick Co. with kilns, drying racks, an incline and an old clay pit, and a large clay pit with a compass rose covers the upper right. Cherry runs off the right edge at the upper right with a row of dwellings and outbuildings along it. The lower right of the sheet is mostly blank lots numbered 523 and 372. Numbers 6, 38 and 40 at the margins refer to the adjoining sheets.
notes: South Pine is South Pine Street in OpenStreetMap; the street printed South is South Avenue today; Fremont, Garfield, Cherry, Colfax and Cedar Dell keep their names with Avenue or Street.
Eighteen junctions were used (RMSE 2.9 m, leave-one-out 3.5 m, about 3.99 px per foot); residuals grow to 3 to 5 metres at the far left (Grove, South) and far right (South East Avenue).

sheet-40-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 40 is the main map of the district south of sheet 39, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned about fifteen degrees from north. Pamphylia Avenue crosses the top, with Baltimore Avenue about a third of the way down, Morris Avenue at the left and Sharp Avenue about the middle of the sheet. South Avenue, South Pine, Spruce and Colfax run from top to bottom, with Grove at the left edge. The upper left blocks carry rows of frame dwellings on South Avenue and the streets east of it, with a few poultry houses and a building marked cement block mfg. and electric power, and lot numbers 218, 373 and 374. Below Baltimore Avenue the streets are laid out in outline across large parcels numbered 376, 528, 529, 530 and 531, with only a scattering of dwellings along South Avenue and the left side; several of the cross streets, among them Colfax and Cone, are marked not open. At the lower left a cement block works with its power house and a number of dwellings stand along South Avenue and the streets east of it. The inset box at the lower right, with Willow, East Railroad Avenue and the Preston Silica Co., is a separate part and is not covered here. Numbers 39 and 40 and the lot numbers 416 and 525 at the left margin refer to adjacent sheets.
notes: South Pine is Pine Street South or South Pine Street in OpenStreetMap; South East Avenue is the street printed S. East Av. at the top right edge.
Fifteen junctions were used (RMSE 1.4 m, leave-one-out 1.8 m, about 3.90 px per foot); no control lies in the bottom third, so the lower part rests on the fit.
The inset at the lower right (Willow, East Railroad Avenue, Preston Silica Co.; its own north arrow points straight up) has no junction with a modern street and is not georeferenced.

sheet-41-1.description: The main part of sheet 41 shows the village of Fairton in Fairfield Township, noted on the sheet as located three and a half miles south-east of Bridgeton City Hall. It is drawn at 100 feet to an inch and turned on the page, with north towards the upper left. Main Street runs down the sheet from the top edge, crosses Rattlesnake Gut on a bridge and turns along the bottom of the sheet past the Methodist Episcopal church, with roads leaving it at both lower corners. Bridgeton Road and Church Street lead west from Main Street; to the east Railroad Avenue and Elmer Avenue run off towards the railroad, joined by Wilson Street and an unnamed cross street. The houses are frame dwellings on long lots. Named buildings include the Fairfield Presbyterian Church, the Fairton Public School, boat building sheds on the bank of Mill Creek, the Diament Bros canning factory beside the railroad and its passenger depot at the upper right, the vacant shed of the Fairton Sand and Clay Co, and greenhouses near Wilson Street. Mill Creek and the Cohansey River bound the village on the west and south-west, and Rattlesnake Gut crosses it from the east. A boxed area at the right of the sheet is a separate inset showing Main Street further north (part 2).
notes: Bridgeton Road is Bridgeton Fairton Road today; Railroad Avenue with the street joining it to Main Street is Ramah Road; Wilson is Buck Street; Church is Church Lane; the unnamed cross street between Railroad and Elmer Avenues is Clark Street.
The road leaving Main Street at the lower left is Back Neck Road; the junction at the lower right is Main Street with Cedarville, Lummis Mill and Rockville Roads.
Fitted scale 3.82 px/ft, about 5 percent smaller than the Bridgeton sheets at 100 ft.

sheet-41-2.description: The inset of sheet 41, boxed by a heavy line at the right of the sheet, continues Main Street in Fairton northward beyond the top edge of the main part; the sheet number 41 printed at its lower end matches the 41 printed at the top of Main Street on the main part. It is drawn at 100 feet to an inch at about the same orientation, with north towards the upper left. A single street, Main Street, 60 feet wide, runs down the middle of the inset between blocks 601 on the west and 606 on the east, divided into deep house lots. A few frame dwellings with outbuildings and auto houses stand along both frontages; there are no cross streets, industries or public buildings. The rest of the box is blank lot land.
notes: No street junction in the inset: placed by one point carried from the top of part 1, assuming the inset continues Main Street without a gap, at the scale of part 1 and its rotation. Low confidence.
